nodes.text: PRINCIPLES OF LYMPHEDEMA

• Lymphedema is a potential side effect after the treatment of cancer resulting from damage to the lymphatic system. Approximately 3 in 4 cases of lymphedema are diagnosed within 3 years of treatment; however, it can develop anytime in the life of the survivor. Depending on stage of diagnosis, lymphedema can be an acute or chronic condition. It can impact any area of the body (eg, arms, legs, face, trunk, groin). • Swelling on the same side as the cancer treatment is a universal symptom of lymphedema. Additional initial symptoms may include sensation of heaviness, fatigue, fullness or tightness in the skin, or pain. Symptoms including decreased range of motion or function and thickening of the skin may occur in later stages. • Survivors who had surgery, radiation, or chemoradiation to the axillary, supraclavicular, cervical, or pelvic inguinal lymph node system are at risk for the development of lymphedema. Sentinel node biopsy also increases the risk of lymphedema, although it poses less risk than complete dissection. • BMI ≥30 kg/m, localized infection, increased number of nodes removed, and higher initial extent of disease raise the risk of lymphedema development. When appropriate, weight management may be considered for individuals with obesity. • When possible, pretreatment baseline objective measurements should be obtained for patients with treatment-related or individual risk factors. Validated volumetric tools, such as perometry, 3D camera or tape measure/girth measures (which may be converted to volumetric measures), and/or tools that measure extracellular fluid, such as bioimpedance spectroscopy, are recommended. • Early detection/diagnosis and early referral are key for optimal lymphedema management because stages 0 and 1 are reversible, whereas stages 2 and 3 are less responsive to treatment. Therefore, survivors at risk for lymphedema should be regularly screened for lymphedema by symptom assessment, clinical exam, and validated volumetric tools and/or tools that measure extracellular fluid. Patients should be educated about early symptoms and signs of lymphedema including fullness, tightness, heaviness, and pain. • Lymphedema may cause or exacerbate psychological distress (SANXDE-1). • Survivors at risk for lymphedema and those with lymphedema are at a higher risk of localized infection in the affected area. These infections can require hospitalization for IV antibiotics. Therefore, survivors with or at risk for lymphedema should be educated to inform their medical provider immediately for signs of infection in the affected area. • Progressive weight training under supervision and physical activity are not associated with exacerbation or development of lymphedema. • Observational studies have demonstrated that air travel, venipuncture, and blood pressure measurement (via arm cuff) are not associated with development of lymphedema, and precautionary measures are likely unnecessary. In the absence of high-level data, the Panel recommends medical procedures such as venipuncture and blood pressure measurements be done on the non–at-risk limb; however, if necessary, procedures may be done using the at-risk limb. More research is needed to determine the effect of these procedures on the risk of lymphedema. Similar studies have not been conducted in individuals with lymphedema. The Panel recommends avoidance of venipuncture and blood pressure measurement (via arm cuff) procedures in any limb with lymphedema. Patients with bilateral upper extremity lymphedema should consult their physician to explore safe alternatives for venipuncture and blood pressure monitoring, aiming to minimize the risk of exacerbating swelling. Strategies may include using smaller-gauge needles, avoiding tourniquets, and selecting alternative sites for blood pressure measurement or blood draws.

nodes.text: Follow-up with treatment team as clinically indicated
GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF PAIN MANAGEMENT

• Comprehensive pain assessment should be done to determine the etiology of the pain. If the pain is new and acute, differential diagnosis should include cancer recurrence or progressive disease. If the pain is chronic, a specific pain syndrome should be identified if possible. • 	Conduct a discussion with the patient and caregivers regarding realistic treatment goals, including improvement in function, minimizing side effects of pain regimen and, if on opioids, safe opioid use, storage, and disposal. • 	New pain in a cancer survivor should prompt an evaluation, with one of the differential diagnoses being a cancer recurrence or progressive disease. Non-cancer pain in cancer survivors should be treated congruent with pain diagnosis, with opioids remaining the last resort. Consider referring to primary care service for management of non-cancer pain. • Use a multimodality approach to pain management if those resources are available. • 	Non-opioid adjuvant analgesics are appropriate as primary therapy for many pain syndromes. • 	Non-pharmacologic interventions can be used as the sole treatment for pain, or as adjuncts to pharmacologic therapy. Physical modalities (heat, cold, massage, acupuncture, physical therapy, or occupational therapy) are useful and should be considered for some pain syndromes. Hypnosis, meditation, acupuncture, cognitive restructuring, and behavioral activation can be considered to control pain and maximize function. • Opioid treatment is sometimes necessary, and the lowest appropriate dose should be used for the shortest amount of time possible. • 	Psychological support of the survivor with chronic pain is necessary, and referral to psychosocial services should be considered for survivors in distress (SANXDE-1). • 	Consider referral to a specialist for survivors who might benefit from further pain interventions. This could include referral to interventional pain, physical medicine and rehabilitation, palliative care, pain specialist, urology, gynecology, orthopedic surgery, gastroenterology, or other appropriate consultants. If these resources are available, consider referral as early as possible during the course of treatment planning. • Opioids and pregnancy: Ensure appropriate opioid prescribing and screening for opioid use disorder (OUD) for survivors of childbearing potential. If a survivor on chronic opioids is pregnant or wants to become pregnant, do not stop opioids abruptly but coordinate further pain management with the obstetrician. If the survivor has OUD and takes buprenorphine for addiction and/or pain, provide access to addiction services without stopping buprenorphine. OUD can cause preterm birth, stillbirth, and neonatal abstinence syndrome. • The Panel acknowledges the legalization of medical cannabis for various conditions in multiple states. However, there are presently not enough data to make any guideline recommendations regarding use in cancer survivors. • Also see the NCCN Guidelines for Adult Cancer Pain.

nodes.text: • When opioids are appropriate and necessary, establish treatment goals with survivors and caregivers and use the lowest effective opioid dose for the shortest period of time possible. • Provide survivor and caregiver education on safe opioid use, risks including risk of psychological and/or physical addiction, safe storage, and disposal. • Consider prescribing naloxone and educate the patient and the caregivers on its use. Instruct caregivers to call 911 Emergency Service if naloxone is administered. • Functional outcomes are important measures for patients on opioid therapy. The expected outcome (ie, improvement in function and/or pain) and terms of monitoring for outcomes, adherence, and safety should be clearly discussed with survivors and caregivers, agreed upon, and documented upon initiation and continuation of chronic therapy. Consider establishing pain treatment agreements/contracts in consultation with state and/or institutional requirements. Pain treatment agreements can be a useful tool in the overall strategy to manage opioid use and long-term pain in survivors. • Re-evaluate the effectiveness, safety, and necessity of opioids at regular intervals. If the expected outcome is not achieved, other treatment alternatives should be considered. If opioids are no longer appropriate, recommend gradual tapering of opioids to help avoid symptoms of withdrawal (see Opioid Principles, Prescribing, Initiation, Titration, Maintenance, and Safety; Principles of Opioid Dose Reduction in Cancer Pain Management in the NCCN Guidelines for Adult Cancer Pain). • Address medical-related issues due to chronic or high-dose opioids. Endocrine/hypopituitary abnormalities

nodes.text: Menopause • Many survivors may experience symptoms whether or not they have ovarian function. • In survivors with prior chemotherapy or pelvic radiation exposure or survivors on tamoxifen, serial estradiol levels may be useful to confirm current menopausal status. • In non-cancer populations, primary ovarian insufficiency or early menopause may be associated with specific menopause-related health risks (see below). There are limited data in cancer survivors. • Peri- or premenopausal survivors For survivors who have become amenorrheic and later develop bleeding, serial estradiol levels can be useful to determine return of ovarian function. Other markers including follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), and inhibin may provide additional information on ovarian status in cancer survivors with prior chemotherapy or those on tamoxifen, but alone are not reliable to ensure menopausal status. Survivors who have become amenorrheic and are sexually active should be counseled on the need for contraception to prevent unintended pregnancy if they do not meet the definition of menopause and if their sexual activity could result in pregnancy. Menopause is defined as no menses for one year in the absence of prior chemotherapy or tamoxifen use, or no menses after surgical removal of all ovarian tissue. Menopausal Signs and Symptoms • Vasomotor symptoms (ie, hot flashes/night sweats) • Vaginal dryness • 	Urogenital symptoms • 	Sexual dysfunction

MHT is generally contraindicated in survivors of hormonally mediated cancers. Custom-compounded bioidentical hormone therapy is not recommended. There is a lack of data supporting claims that custom-compounded bioidentical hormones are a safer and more effective alternative to standard hormone therapies. In fact, they may be harmful.
Non-Hormonal Pharmacologic Treatments and Dosing (SHRS-A).

Survivors often use herbal supplements for vasomotor symptom management. However, some supplements may interfere with hormonal cancer treatments, and routine use of supplements is not recommended (SSUP-1). Providers should encourage survivors to discuss such therapies prior to use. Dietary supplements are not evaluated by the FDA for purity, safety, or effectiveness before they are marketed. Therefore potential harms exist, including toxicities and drug interactions (Discussion).
Drinking alcohol may cause hot flashes. Individual responses to alcohol may vary. If alcohol is a trigger, consider limiting intake.

• The risks of treatment-induced infertility should be discussed with all reproductive-aged survivors at the time of cancer diagnosis. • 	Survivor-centered care is important. The survivor’s goals regarding fertility and discussions regarding the risks of treatment-induced infertility should be discussed and documented in the medical chart. • Prior to initiation of cancer treatments, available options for fertility preservation should be discussed and/or referrals made to the appropriate specialists for those patients wishing to preserve fertility. • 	Fertility preservation procedures prior to cancer treatment are the most effective way to preserve fertility in cancer survivors. Fertility cryopreservation procedures include in vitro fertilization (IVF) with oocyte and/or embryo cryopreservation, ovarian tissue cryopreservation, and sperm cryopreservation. Data show that ovarian tissue cryopreservation is currently only about 40% successful in centers with this expertise. There is a much greater success with traditional IVF with oocyte or embryo cryopreservation. In addition to fertility preservation procedures, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists should be offered during chemotherapy to breast cancer survivors in order to preserve ovarian function. • Some emerging evidence suggests that ovarian tissue cryopreservation after aggressive cancer treatment can result in viable tissue and live births following transplantation. Testicular sperm extraction and intracytoplasmic sperm injection are methods that can help post- treatment survivors with minimal sperm achieve pregnancy. • If possible, reproductive organs should be shielded during RT. • If survivors have a change in their cancer treatment, the impact of treatment on potential infertility should be discussed again and/or referrals made to the appropriate specialists. • 	Once cancer treatment is complete, clinicians and survivors should not assume that the survivor is infertile, and survivors interested in fertility should be assessed by a fertility specialist. • 	For most survivors of breast cancer, pregnancy is considered safe and the hormonal environment associated with pregnancy is not thought to increase the risk of breast cancer recurrence. Prior breast cancer treatment does not increase the future risk of congenital malformations General recommendations have traditionally been to wait until the survivor is disease free for 2 years before attempting to conceive, whether naturally or via assisted reproductive technologies, because of the higher risk of recurrence within that time. • For additional information regarding fertility preservation for patients with cancer, see: NCCN Guidelines for Adolescent and Young Adult (AYA) Oncology NCCN Guidelines for Breast Cancer 1	Su HI, Lacchetti C, Letourneau J, et al. nodes.text: GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF SLEEP

Importance of Sleep Health • Sleep is composed of a complex set of neurobehavioral states that regulate a broad range of brain and systemic functions in cells and tissues. Sleep and wake cycles are regulated by a dynamic interaction between sleep homeostatic and circadian processes, and their proper alignment determines sleep quality. There is very strong evidence that sleep is critical for overall health and quality of life. • Sleep and circadian rhythm disturbances increase the risk for cardiovascular, metabolic, neurologic, psychiatric, immunologic disorders, and certain types of cancer. Conversely, chronic medical and mental health disorders negatively affect sleep quality, resulting in a bidirectional relationship between sleep and general health and well-being.

nodes.text: Healthy Sleep • Sleep health is a multidimensional construct, consisting of duration, timing, regularity and satisfaction. Healthy sleep behaviors include getting enough sleep on a regular basis. Experts recommend at least 7 hours per night for adults. Keeping a regular sleep schedule, even on weekends, helps maintain a regular sleep-wake cycle.

nodes.text: Sleep in Cancer Survivors • Sleep and wake disturbances are common in the general population, but the prevalence is significantly higher in patients with cancer and survivors, ranging from 30% to over 80%. Moreover, sleep problems can persist for years after completion of cancer treatment. • Multiple factors contribute to the higher prevalence of sleep disturbances, including psychological stress, mood disorders (depression and anxiety), environmental/behavioral factors, and side effects of cancer treatment. Cancer treatment-related psychological and physical side effects such as chronic pain, lymphedema, nocturia, and menopausal symptoms are commonly associated with insomnia. Both treatment- related iron deficiency and neuropathy can increase vulnerability for restless legs syndrome, and menopause-related hormonal changes increase risk for vasomotor symptoms that disturb sleep, insomnia disorders, and obstructive sleep apnea. • Given the critical relationship between sleep, health, and quality of life, identifying and addressing sleep disorders are of high importance in cancer survivorship. The consequences of sleep disruption and sleep disorders on impaired cognitive, cardiometabolic, immune, and mental health are particularly relevant to cancer survivors, a population at increased risk for these conditions. Improving sleep may not only improve quality of life, it may also improve overall health and resilience in this vulnerable population.

Assessment and Treatment • Diagnosis of most sleep disorders relies on a careful history, is clinically based, and typically does not require diagnostic procedures. Nonetheless, sleep studies are necessary to establish the diagnosis of sleep apnea, narcolepsy, and some parasomnias. For some disorders (eg, parasomnias), a specialized in-lab polysomnogram (PSG) is required for diagnosis. For narcolepsy, the multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) is required to establish the diagnosis. In addition to in-lab PSG, home-based sleep studies are increasingly being used for diagnosis of sleep apnea • Most patients with sleep disorders will benefit from recommendations that promote healthy sleep behaviors, otherwise known as sleep hygiene (SSD-A). Of note, sleep hygiene alone has not been shown to be an effective non-pharmacological approach for the treatment of chronic insomnia, in which a more comprehensive approach with cognitive behavior therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is recommended as a first-line treatment. (SSD-4). • Pharmacological approaches may be used as adjunctive therapy in sleep disorders, most notably with insomnia, restless legs, hypersomnia and some parasomnias, such as rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (SSD-4). Given the high comorbidity of sleep disturbances with medical, neurologic, and psychiatric disease, clinicians must be aware of the safety profile of sedatives and stimulants and guard against adverse drug interactions.

Sleep disorders such as insomnia, RLS, and sleep apnea are more prevalent in menopausal individuals. Hormonal changes, vasomotor symptoms, and lifestyle contribute to these sleep disturbance(s). For menopausal survivors for whom insomnia is associated with vasomotor symptoms, treatment of vasomotor symptoms can improve sleep, which can in turn help with vasomotor symptoms. The best evidence for improving sleep dysfunction related to vasomotor symptoms is for use of MHT. Other strategies could be also considered for patients unable to be on MHT (SHRS-4) (Mirer AG, et al. Menopause 2017;24:157-162; Seeman MV. nodes.text: GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF WORKING AND RETURNING TO WORK AFTER A CANCER DIAGNOSIS
lines: GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF WORKING AND RETURNING TO WORK AFTER A CANCER DIAGNOSIS

nodes.text: • These recommendations related to working and returning to work apply to survivors during and following active treatment as well as persons living chronically with cancer. Discussions about work are ideally best had before treatment begins so that treatment recommendations can take work needs into consideration if possible. • Symptoms affecting work may wax and wane with a survivor’s treatments or disease status, especially if they are living chronically with cancer or the consequences of cancer treatment. Some survivors may continue to work through treatment while others might start and stop working more than once. • The existing literature focuses on unemployment and/or those who do not return to work during active treatment. However, underemployment and/or work limitations due to cancer or side effects from treatment are also common. • Employment helps to protect survivors from financial toxicity and, at least in the United States, is frequently tied to health insurance access. This can be a main reason survivors work even when/if they are not fully recovered. Financial toxicity is common among cancer survivors. Consider screening and referral to financial counselor and/or social worker as early as possible. The United States does not have federally mandated paid sick leave for survivors or their caregivers. The absence of paid sick leave may affect survivors' ability to adhere to treatment regimens and surveillance and may affect their ability to maintain employment during treatment. • Employment is an important source of personal interaction, normalcy, and social support. The psychosocial effects/advantages derived from work may include a sense of purpose, emotional well-being, link to identity, improved quality of life, connection with others, and distraction. • Some populations are at increased risk for difficulties related to work (based on factors such as gender, age, race, ethnicity, cancer type, cancer stage, rural residence, educational attainment, job type and demands, work environment, etc). The increased difficulties in these populations are more likely for survivors with physically or cognitively demanding jobs or jobs with limited flexibility in scheduling or tasks. Additionally, patients with cancer may experience discrimination as a result of diagnosis/illness, and this may be a consideration for some individuals in decisions surrounding employment. • Survivors should be offered information to help them understand their likely ability to work, take into account their finances and personal/ family needs, and discuss potential work accommodations with their employers. • Clinicians should regularly re-evaluate work-related concerns post active cancer treatment or for persons living chronically with cancer. Periodically identify goals and barriers regarding work with survivor (SWORK-3). A team approach may be needed. Consider early involvement of social work, primary care, physical therapy/occupational therapy, cancer rehabilitation, and/or career counseling services, if available. Employment disability forms are not typically well-suited to cancer. However, clinicians should consider the survivor’s needs for flexibility in tasks and hours, and other workplace accommodations as a starting point for filling out the necessary forms.

bmi_kg_m2.definition: Body mass index from the most recent measured height and weight.

gender_identity.definition: Survivor's gender identity as stated in the case.

reproductive_age.definition: Survivor is of reproductive age or has childbearing potential.

prior_chemotherapy.definition: Survivor has received chemotherapy in the past.

prior_chest_radiation.definition: Survivor has received chest or mantle radiation in the past.

prior_pelvic_radiation.definition: Survivor has received pelvic radiation in the past.

cardiotoxicity_risk_history.definition: Survivor has potentially cardiotoxic treatment history (anthracycline or chest irradiation), or has hypertension, coronary artery disease, diabetes, or a family history of cardiomyopathy.

current_adt.definition: Survivor is currently receiving androgen deprivation therapy.

current_chemo_rt_or_pdt.definition: Survivor is currently undergoing chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or photodynamic therapy.

cancer_treatment_change.definition: There has been a change in the survivor's cancer treatment.

disease_free_years.definition: Years since the survivor was last known to be free of disease.

prostate_cancer_no_recurrence.definition: Survivor has prostate cancer with no evidence of recurrent disease.

vitamin_deficiency_risk_from_treatment.definition: Survivor's cancer treatment places them at risk of vitamin deficiency.

anti_b_cell_therapy.definition: Survivor has received anti-B-cell antibody therapy.

splenectomy_or_functional_asplenia.definition: Survivor has had a splenectomy or has functional asplenia.

months_since_immunosuppressive_exposure.definition: Months since the most recent exposure to cytotoxic chemotherapy, monoclonal antibodies, radiation (for example splenic RT), corticosteroids, cellular therapy, or hematopoietic cell transplant. Use 0 if the exposure is ongoing.

stated_recent_immunosuppressive_exposure.definition: The case explicitly states that the survivor has ongoing or recent (under 3 months) immunosuppressive exposure. Used only when the case states the classification directly.

vaccines_completed_before_treatment.definition: Indicated vaccines were given before cancer treatment started.

hct_received.definition: Survivor has received a hematopoietic cell transplant (peripheral blood stem cell, bone marrow, or cord blood).

structural_heart_disease.definition: Echocardiogram or other testing shows structural heart disease (LV dysfunction, LV hypertrophy, valvular disease, LV dilatation or wall thinning, or previous myocardial infarction).

heart_failure_signs_symptoms.definition: Survivor has signs or symptoms of heart failure.

advanced_refractory_heart_failure.definition: Advanced structural heart disease with marked heart failure symptoms at rest despite maximal medical therapy, requiring specialized interventions.

significant_comorbidity_present.definition: Survivor has at least one significant comorbidity or physical limitation that could affect exercise.

arthritis_or_musculoskeletal_issue.definition: Survivor has arthritis or a musculoskeletal problem.

recent_lung_or_major_abdominal_surgery.definition: Survivor has a history of lung surgery or major abdominal surgery.

cardiopulmonary_comorbidity.definition: Survivor has COPD, congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease, or cardiomyopathy.

severe_nutritional_deficiency.definition: Survivor has a severe nutritional deficiency.

severe_fatigue.definition: Survivor is clinically described as having severe fatigue.

worsening_health_condition.definition: Survivor's health condition is worsening or changing (for example lymphedema exacerbation).

physical_activity_moderate_equiv_min_wee.definition: Weekly minutes of physical activity, where vigorous minutes count double (moderate minutes plus 2 times vigorous minutes).

exercise_tolerated.definition: Survivor is tolerating the current or suggested exercise prescription.

exercise_progressing.definition: Survivor is progressing toward incremental exercise goals.

fatigue_score.definition: Self-reported fatigue severity on a 0 to 10 scale (0 = no fatigue, 10 = worst fatigue imaginable).

fatigue_after_adjuvant_or_worsening.definition: Fatigue initially presents months after adjuvant therapy or worsens over that period.

iron_b12_or_folate_deficiency.definition: Survivor has an iron, vitamin B12, or folate deficiency.

depressive_symptom_count.definition: Number of DSM-style depressive symptoms present (depressed mood, anhedonia, weight change, sleep change, psychomotor change, low energy, worthlessness, poor concentration, thoughts of death or suicide).

depressive_symptom_duration_weeks.definition: Duration of the depressive symptoms, in weeks, present at least half of the time.

anxiety_symptom_count.definition: Number of generalized anxiety symptoms present (restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance).

anxiety_symptom_duration_months.definition: Duration of excessive anxiety and worry, in months.

excessive_difficult_to_control_worry.definition: Survivor has excessive anxiety and worry that is difficult to control.

panic_symptom_count.definition: Number of panic attack symptoms present during a sudden intense fear episode.

mania_symptom_count.definition: Number of mania symptoms present (expansive or irritable mood, increased energy, and related signs).

safety_risk_present.definition: Survivor presents a safety risk (for example suicidal ideation with intent or plan).

ptsd_symptoms_present.definition: Survivor has PTSD symptoms after an exposure to a traumatic event.

traumatic_event_exposure.definition: Survivor was exposed to a traumatic event (directly experienced, witnessed, learned of it occurring to a close family member or friend, or repeated or extreme exposure to aversive details), including a cancer diagnosis or treatment.

ptsd_symptom_categories_count.definition: Number of the 4 PTSD symptom categories listed in SANXDE-4 in which the survivor has at least one symptom.

ptsd_symptom_duration_months.definition: Duration of the PTSD symptoms, in months.

ptsd_symptoms_cause_significant_distress.definition: The PTSD symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment.

distress_impairs_quality_of_life.definition: Distress, anxiety, depression, or trauma symptoms are impairing quality of life or the ability to cope.

identifiable_stressor_present.definition: An identifiable stressor (for example fear of recurrence, body changes, or other effects of cancer and treatment, or a significant loss) is present.

stressor_onset_months_ago.definition: Months since onset of the identifiable stressor.

emotional_behavioral_symptoms_in_respons.definition: Survivor has emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor.

mood_screen_result.definition: Result of the mood screening questions.

recurrent_cancer_related_worry.definition: Survivor has recurrent worry, fear, or intrusive images related to cancer events.

compulsive_behaviors.definition: Survivor has compulsive repetitive thoughts or behaviors aimed at reducing anxiety.

needs_observed_for_psychosocial_support.definition: Clinician observes psychosocial needs in the survivor.

symptoms_persistent_or_increased.definition: Survivor's symptoms (anxiety, depression, stress, or related symptoms) are persistent or have increased at follow-up.

insomnia_symptoms_present.definition: Survivor has difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early, or poor sleep quality.

insomnia_duration_months.definition: Duration of insomnia symptoms, in months.

insomnia_nights_per_week.definition: Number of nights per week with insomnia symptoms.

insomnia_daytime_impairment_or_distress.definition: Insomnia symptoms cause decreased daytime functioning, poor quality of life, or distress to the survivor.

sleep_apnea_or_snoring_features.definition: Survivor has observed apneas or snoring, or features suggestive of sleep-disordered breathing.

nocturia_present.definition: Survivor has nocturia (waking at night to urinate).

circadian_rhythm_disorder.definition: Survivor has a circadian rhythm disorder.

sexual_health_screen_result.definition: Result of the sexual health screening questions.

ongoing_sexual_function_concern.definition: Survivor has ongoing concerns regarding sexual function (a concern is present; no concern is false).

sexual_concern_improved_or_resolved.definition: The sexual function concern has improved or resolved.

climacturia.definition: Survivor has urinary leakage during orgasm (climacturia).

amenorrhea_with_later_bleeding.definition: Survivor who had become amenorrheic later develops vaginal bleeding.

hypogonadism_history.definition: Survivor has symptoms of or a prior history of hypogonadism.

vasomotor_symptoms_disruptive.definition: Hot flashes or night sweats are disruptive to quality of life.

hormone_symptoms_disruptive.definition: Hormone-related symptoms are disruptive to quality of life.

herbal_supplement_for_vasomotor_symptoms.definition: Survivor uses herbal supplements for vasomotor symptoms.

pain_category.definition: Category of pain reported on screening.

pain_onset.definition: Whether the pain is new and acute or chronic.

pain_expected_outcome_achieved.definition: The expected pain or functional outcome of opioid therapy has been achieved.

opioid_duration_months.definition: Months the survivor has been taking opioids continuously or near-continuously.

opioid_mme_per_day.definition: Current daily opioid dose in morphine milligram equivalents (MME) per day.

stated_chronic_or_high_dose_opioid.definition: The case explicitly states that the survivor is on chronic or high-dose opioids. Used only when the case states the classification directly.

aberrant_opioid_use.definition: There is evidence of aberrant opioid-taking behavior or substance use disorder.

opioids_no_longer_appropriate.definition: Opioids are no longer appropriate for the survivor.

opioids_indicated.criteria: When opioids are appropriate and necessary
opioids_indicated.definition: Clinician judges that opioids are appropriate and necessary for the survivor (the guideline's 'if opioids are indicated' condition).

opioid_adverse_effects.definition: Survivor has adverse effects from opioids (constipation, nausea, pruritus, delirium, cognitive impairment, respiratory depression, sedation).

pregnant_or_wants_pregnancy_on_opioids.definition: Survivor on chronic opioids is pregnant or wants to become pregnant.

bilateral_upper_extremity_lymphedema.definition: Survivor has bilateral upper extremity lymphedema.

survivor_at_risk_for_lymphedema.definition: Survivor is at risk for lymphedema, from treatment-related or individual risk factors.

obesity_present.definition: Survivor has obesity. The guideline gives no criteria.

financial_toxicity_present.definition: Survivor reports financial toxicity or financial strain from cancer care.

work_barriers_present.definition: Survivor reports barriers to working (transportation, caregiving, health insurance, job demands).

focal_neurologic_deficit.definition: Survivor has a focal neurologic deficit.

cognitive_impairment_persistent.definition: Cognitive impairment has persisted after treatment.

brain_primary_tumor.definition: Survivor has a primary brain tumor.

stated_high_risk_or_metastatic_brain_dis.definition: The case explicitly states that the survivor has high-risk disease, known metastatic disease, or a brain primary. Used only when the case states the classification directly.

prostate_cancer_history.definition: Survivor has a history of prostate cancer.

prior_cancer_surgery.definition: Survivor has had surgery for a cancer.

supplement_prescribed_by_provider.definition: The supplement is prescribed by a medical provider.

documented_vitamin_deficiency.definition: A vitamin or nutrient deficiency is documented.

inadequate_diet.definition: Survivor's dietary intake is inadequate to meet nutrient needs.

previous_gi_surgery_malabsorption_risk.definition: Survivor has had gastrointestinal surgery that may cause deficiencies (for example Roux-en-Y gastric bypass).

comorbidity_indicating_supplement.definition: Survivor has a comorbidity that indicates supplement use (for example osteoporosis, ophthalmologic disorder, or cirrhosis).

comprehensive_family_history_done.definition: A comprehensive family cancer history, including any prior genetic testing, has been obtained.

family_history_updated_recently.definition: Family cancer history has been updated recently.

genetic_testing_criteria_met.definition: Survivor meets NCCN genetic testing criteria based on the risk assessment.

prior_negative_limited_gene_panel.definition: Survivor had a prior negative genetic test that used a limited set of genes.

no_comprehensive_evaluation_at_diagnosis.definition: Survivor did not have a comprehensive genetic risk evaluation at diagnosis.

annual_assessment_due.definition: A periodic provider assessment is due (at least annually).

special_circumstance_or_risk_factor_for_.criteria: Recommended if some special circumstance or risk factor is present
special_circumstance_or_risk_factor_for_.definition: A special circumstance or risk factor for a vaccine is present (for example functional or anatomic asplenia, lifestyle, upcoming travel, or local epidemic).

values: Survivorship: Anxiety, Depression, Trauma, and Distress
Survivorship: Employment and Return to Work
guideline_section.definition: Which disease or subtype section of this guideline the case belongs to: the disease named in the guideline's page headings that the patient has (e.g. the tumor type or subtype).

weight_category.definition: BMI category used to choose weight management goal (weight gain, maintenance, or loss).

weight_management_goal.definition: Weight management goal from BMI: weight gain if BMI is below 18.5; maintenance if BMI is 18.5 to 24.9 (the target range in SNWM-2); weight loss if BMI is 25 or higher.

activity_guideline_status.definition: Whether weekly physical activity meets the guideline of 150 minutes moderate or equivalent.

pa_adverse_event_risk_factor_present.definition: Survivor has a risk factor for physical activity-induced adverse events: history of lung surgery or major abdominal surgery, ostomy, cardiopulmonary comorbidity, severe nutritional deficiency, or severe fatigue.

fatigue_severity.definition: Fatigue severity category from the 0 to 10 score.

major_depressive_disorder_status.definition: Whether depressive symptoms meet the MDD pattern: at least 5 symptoms for at least 2 weeks.

anxiety_pattern.definition: Anxiety pattern used to choose the diagnostic consideration.

anxiety_symptom_criteria_met.definition: Excessive anxiety and worry that is difficult to control, with at least 3 of the listed anxiety symptoms (SANXDE-3 anxiety diagnosis box).

adjustment_or_other_anxiety_disorder_bra.definition: True when the anxiety criteria are not met because there are fewer than 3 symptoms and/or the symptoms persist less than 6 months (adjustment disorder with anxious or mixed mood, or other anxiety disorder). Exactly 6 months is not under 6 months.

ptsd_criteria_met.definition: PTSD diagnosis pattern: traumatic event exposure, symptoms from each of the 4 categories, symptoms lasting over one month, and clinically significant distress or impairment.

adjustment_disorder_or_distress_pattern.definition: Adjustment disorder or distress pattern: emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor that began within 3 months, or distress that impairs the ability to cope.

mood_screen_positive.definition: A positive response to the mood screening questions (any screen result with an impact on quality of life), which requires further assessment.

adjustment_disorder_severity.definition: Severity of adjustment disorder or distress.

safety_mania_psychosis_status.criteria_source: external: DSM-5 mania and psychosis criteria
safety_mania_psychosis_status.definition: Whether there is a safety risk, mania, or psychosis requiring urgent evaluation.

sleep_duration_adequacy.definition: Whether sleep duration meets the recommendation of at least 7 hours per night.

insomnia_status.definition: Insomnia disorder pattern: symptoms at least 3 months and at least 3 nights per week.

insomnia_problematic.definition: Insomnia disorder that is problematic: symptoms at least 3 months and at least 3 nights per week, causing decreased daytime functioning, poor quality of life, or distress.

cardiac_stage.definition: ACC/AHA-style cardiotoxicity stage (A to D) based on structure and symptoms.

conception_timing_advice.definition: Whether the survivor has reached the traditional 2 years disease-free before attempting conception.

high_risk_or_metastatic_brain_disease.definition: Survivor has high-risk disease, known metastatic disease, or a brain primary. The box does not state high-risk criteria and names no published definition, so this rule covers only the known metastatic disease and brain primary conditions; high-risk disease counts only when the case states it.

non_prostate_cancer_treatment_received.definition: Survivor has received radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or surgery for a malignancy other than prostate cancer (SHRS-2).

menopause_risk_exposure.definition: Survivor with prior chemotherapy or pelvic radiation exposure, or currently on tamoxifen (menopause box, SHRS-1).

peri_premenopausal_amenorrhea_later_blee.definition: Peri- or premenopausal survivor who had become amenorrheic and later develops bleeding (SHRS-1).

peri_premenopausal_amenorrheic_sexually_.definition: Peri- or premenopausal survivor who has become amenorrheic and is sexually active (SHRS-1).

vaginal_or_menopausal_symptoms_present.definition: Menopausal symptoms (disruptive vasomotor symptoms), vaginal dryness, or urogenital symptoms (SSH-2 parent condition).

recent_immunosuppressive_exposure.definition: Ongoing or recent (under 3 months) exposure to cytotoxic chemotherapy, monoclonal antibodies, radiation, corticosteroids, cellular therapy, or hematopoietic cell transplant.

inactivated_vaccine_timing_met.definition: Inactivated or purified-antigen vaccines may be given at least 3 months after cytotoxic chemotherapy or RT, and at least 6 months after HCT.

supplement_indication_present.definition: A supplement indication is present: documented deficiency, inadequate diet, previous GI surgery that may cause deficiency, or a comorbidity indicating supplement use.

chronic_or_high_dose_opioid.definition: Survivor is on chronic or high-dose opioids. The box gives no criteria, so the standard CDC 2016 definitions are used: chronic means opioid use for 3 months or longer; high-dose means 90 MME per day or more.

notes.predicates: Conditions were drafted and reviewed by a language model (model_reviewed), not by clinicians. 'rejected' means the review rejected the draft; the box then needs clinician judgement. 'section_only' means the box only requires the patient to be in the page's guideline section.
notes.coordinates: bbox and line_bboxes are PDF points with the origin at the page's top left; pages[].size gives the page size.
notes.links: page links name a page id from pages[]; a multi-page code such as PROS-F has ids 'PROS-F 1 of 5' ... ; external_guideline links name another guideline's slug.
